claims.text: A workflow coupling machine-learned interatomic potentials with thermodynamic-integration molecular dynamics can accurately predict melting temperatures across diverse high-entropy alloys.
The proposed workflow can predict enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across diverse high-entropy alloys.
Machine-learning interatomic potentials can be deployed in molecular-dynamics simulations of high-entropy alloys.
Robust machine-learning potentials for the proposed HEA family can be trained on ab initio data.
Temperature-ramped MD combined with thermodynamic integration can compute solid-liquid free-energy differences in HEAs.
The simulations can cover temperatures from room temperature to well above the melting point for various HEA compositions.
Calibration against known binary or ternary alloys can serve as an intermediate checkpoint.
Local atomic rearrangements and short-range-order changes during melting mediate the solid-liquid free-energy change.
The simulation captures the effects of lattice distortion and configurational entropy during melting.
The machine-learned potential accurately reproduces interatomic interactions in complex multicomponent HEA environments.
Thermodynamic integration of solid and liquid free energies yields the melting temperature.
The same simulation yields latent heat, derived entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
Machine-learned potentials resolve atomic dynamics better than conventional classical potentials and thereby reduce systematic errors from inadequate local-bonding descriptions.
The workflow is expected to predict melting temperatures within approximately 50 K of experiment.
The workflow is expected to predict fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change within approximately 10% of experiment.
The workflow will perform better quantitatively than conventional potentials optimized for simpler alloys.
Classical potentials calibrated for simpler alloys or empirical rules often produce melting-temperature errors exceeding 100 K and fusion-thermodynamic errors exceeding 10% in HEAs.
The method is most applicable to single-phase solid-solution HEAs in the high-temperature regime.
Phase separation, strong chemical ordering, or competing phases near melting can reduce accuracy when those phenomena are not represented in the training data.
The approach is falsified if, for a majority of tested compositions, melting-temperature errors exceed 100 K or fusion enthalpy, entropy, or volume-change errors exceed 20% relative to experiment.
